## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates expertise in cross-process IPC, memory ordering semantics, and memory reclamation in NUMA environments under realistic contention scenarios.

## Key Concepts
- Cross-process lock-free data structures
- Memory ordering: acquire/release fences and sequence counters
- False sharing prevention through cache-line padding
- Epoch-based reclamation across process boundaries
- NUMA-aware performance optimization
- Microbenchmark design for IPC throughput and latency analysis

## Code Example
```c
typedef struct {
    uint64_t seq;
    uint8_t payload[128];
```

## Implementation Details
The queue uses a circular buffer with sequence numbers to track slot ownership. Each slot has a 64-bit sequence number that ensures proper synchronization between producers and consumers without locks. The padded head/tail indices prevent false sharing on cache lines.

## Performance Considerations
NUMA-aware placement of shared memory regions minimizes cross-node memory access. The spin-wait approach is suitable for high-throughput scenarios where the queue is rarely empty or full.

## Benchmarking Strategy
Design microbenchmarks that vary producer/consumer ratios (1:1, 1:N, N:1) and measure p95/p99 latencies under different contention levels. Validate data integrity by embedding checksums in payloads and verifying them after each operation.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests fundamentals of low-level synchronization, memory ordering, and cache performance with a simple, fair mechanism that beginners can implement and reason about.

## Key Concepts
- Atomic operations and memory_order semantics
- Fairness via ticketing
- False sharing and cache-line padding
- Simple microbenchmarks to compare contention behavior

## Code Example
```javascript
// Pseudo-C: structure and lock/unlock in C with atomics
#include <stdatomic.h>
typedef struct { alignas(64) atomic_uint64_t next_ticket; atomic_uint64_t now_serving; } ticket_lock_t;
void lock(ticket_lock_t *l){ uint64_t t = atomic_fetch_add(&l->next_ticket,1); while (atomic_load(&l->now_serving) != t) {} }
void unlock(ticket_lock_t *l){ atomic_fetch_add(&l->now_serving,1); }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you modify for multiple locks to reduce contention?
- How would you detect and fix starvation in adversarial workloads?

questions.explanation: This question assesses practical knowledge of lock-free data structure design, work-stealing schedulers, memory ordering semantics on x86-64, and performance optimization for NUMA-aware systems. It tests understanding of the Chase-Lev deque, ABA prevention techniques, and the ability to translate algorithmic concepts into correct, high-performance code. Strong candidates will also discuss cache-line padding, false sharing avoidance, and benchmark methodology.
